packet.headline_seed: We are chasing Ebola virus - it is ahead of us, WHO warns
packet.description_seed: Infection rates are high, adding to concern that authorities are struggling to get to grips with the disease.

what: We are chasing Ebola virus - it is ahead of us, WHO warns

clean_source_blocks.text: Health workers need to be fully protected as the virus can spread from touching bodily fluids. The latest Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo began at least three months before it was officially declared - meaning the health authorities are still playing catch-up, the World Health Organization (WHO) has warned. More than 1,900 people have died from the virus since that declaration on 15 May, making this the second-worst Ebola outbreak ever. Infection rates are still high, adding to the concern that the authorities are struggling to get to grips with the spread of the disease. The epicentre of this outbreak of the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, is in the east of DR Congo where insecurity has hampered control efforts. There is also no approved vaccine or any recognised therapeutic drugs, making treating Bundibugyo harder.
Infection rates are high, adding to concern that authorities are struggling to get to grips with the disease.

"We are chasing the virus, the virus is ahead of us," WHO Africa director Dr Mohamed Janabi said at a news conference in the city of Bunia, which is at the heart of this outbreak. He cited research showing that the virus started spreading in February and was initially misdiagnosed as malaria or typhoid. Janabi also said that, in part because of insecurity, health workers are only reaching about 30% of the cases with the rest dying at home. Traditional burial practices – where mourners touch the deceased's body - and a suspicion of health authorities in some communities have also made things difficult. But there are now several dedicated treatment centres in the east of DR Congo and people are getting diagnosed much more quickly.

According to the latest figures released by local authorities, the DRC had recorded 4,209 confirmed cases, including 1,916 deaths, as of Aug. 7. Cases have been reported in Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uele, and Tshopo provinces in the country's east. "We are chasing the virus. The virus is ahead of us," Janabi said, pointing to the prolonged period during which transmission may have gone undetected. Some infections during the early phase of the outbreak may have initially been attributed to other illnesses, including malaria and typhoid, contributing to delays in recognizing the extent of Ebola transmission, Janabi said, warning of prolonged undetected circulation. He also noted that the virus is spreading faster than initially anticipated, while the current outbreak differs from previous outbreaks caused by the Bundibugyo virus in Uganda in 2007 and the DRC in 2012.

Health workers need to be fully protected as the virus can spread from touching bodily fluids.

The latest Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo began at least three months before it was officially declared - meaning the health authorities are still playing catch-up, the World Health Organization (WHO) has warned.

More than 1,900 people have died from the virus since that declaration on 15 May, making this the second-worst Ebola outbreak ever.

Infection rates are still high, adding to the concern that the authorities are struggling to get to grips with the spread of the disease.

The epicentre of this outbreak of the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, is in the east of DR Congo where insecurity has hampered control efforts.

There is also no approved vaccine or any recognised therapeutic drugs, making treating Bundibugyo harder.

"We are chasing the virus, the virus is ahead of us," WHO Africa director Dr Mohamed Janabi said at a news conference in the city of Bunia, which is at the heart of this outbreak.

He cited research showing that the virus started spreading in February and was initially misdiagnosed as malaria or typhoid.

Janabi also said that, in part because of insecurity, health workers are only reaching about 30% of the cases with the rest dying at home.

Traditional burial practices – where mourners touch the deceased's body - and a suspicion of health authorities in some communities have also made things difficult.

But there are now several dedicated treatment centres in the east of DR Congo and people are getting diagnosed much more quickly.

So far there have been 4,294 confirmed cases and 1,960 deaths, DR Congo's health ministry has said.

The largest recorded outbreak was in West Africa between 2014 and 2016 when 11,325 people died.

[Lähde: Xinhuanet | URL: http://www.chinaview.cn/20260810/23f0deaa581846638e35b110141fd9b6/c.html]
KINSHASA, Aug. 10 (Xinhua) -- The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) may have begun as early as February, months before it was officially declared in May, according to genetic sequencing studies, a senior World Health Organization (WHO) official said Monday.

Speaking at a press conference in Bunia, capital of the eastern Ituri Province and the epicenter of the outbreak, WHO Regional Director for Africa Mohamed Yakub Janabi said genetic sequencing indicated that the virus had likely been circulating for months before the outbreak was detected.

The DRC officially declared outbreaks of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus on May 15.

According to the latest figures released by local authorities, the DRC had recorded 4,209 confirmed cases, including 1,916 deaths, as of Aug. 7. Cases have been reported in Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uele, and Tshopo provinces in the country's east.

"We are chasing the virus. The virus is ahead of us," Janabi said, pointing to the prolonged period during which transmission may have gone undetected.

Some infections during the early phase of the outbreak may have initially been attributed to other illnesses, including malaria and typhoid, contributing to delays in recognizing the extent of Ebola transmission, Janabi said, warning of prolonged undetected circulation.

He also noted that the virus is spreading faster than initially anticipated, while the current outbreak differs from previous outbreaks caused by the Bundibugyo virus in Uganda in 2007 and the DRC in 2012.

Meanwhile, the response teams are still detecting only a fraction of infections early enough, Janabi said, adding that around 60 to 70 percent of deaths were reported outside the treatment centers.

On Aug. 7, a WHO technical advisory group recommended that the Ervebo vaccine be prioritized for inclusion in a randomized clinical trial in the context of the ongoing outbreak.

payload.title: WHO: Ebolan torjunta laahaa viruksen leviämisen perässä Kongossa
payload.summary: Bundibugyo-ebolavirus levisi kuukausia ennen epidemian virallista julistamista Kongon demokraattisessa tasavallassa. Elokuun 7. päivään mennessä oli vahvistettu 4 209 tartuntaa ja 1 916 kuolemaa.
payload.content:
Kongon demokraattisen tasavallan itäosissa leviävä Bundibugyo-ebolaviruksen aiheuttama epidemia ehti Maailman terveysjärjestön WHO:n mukaan jatkua vähintään kolme kuukautta ennen kuin se julistettiin virallisesti 15. toukokuuta. Virus alkoi tutkimusten perusteella levitä jo helmikuussa, ja tartuntoja todetaan edelleen runsaasti. WHO varoittaa torjunnan etenevän yhä viruksen leviämistä jäljessä. Paikallisviranomaisten 7. elokuuta julkistamien tietojen mukaan maassa oli todettu 4 209 vahvistettua tartuntaa, joista 1 916 oli johtanut kuolemaan. Tapauksia oli raportoitu Iturin, Pohjois-Kivun, Etelä-Kivun, Haut-Uélén ja Tshopon maakunnissa. Yli 1 900 ihmistä on kuollut epidemian virallisen julistamisen jälkeen, ja kyseessä on toiseksi vakavin koskaan raportoitu ebolaepidemia.

Varhaisia tartuntoja luultiin muiksi sairauksiksi

WHO:n Afrikan-alueen johtaja Mohamed Janabi kertoi Buniassa järjestetyssä tiedotustilaisuudessa, että epidemian alkuvaiheen tartuntoja diagnosoitiin malariaksi tai lavantaudiksi. Tämä viivästytti epidemian laajuuden tunnistamista ja mahdollisti viruksen huomaamattoman leviämisen. Janabin mukaan virus leviää myös nopeammin kuin epidemian alkuvaiheessa arvioitiin. Bundibugyo-virus voi tarttua kehon nesteiden välityksellä, joten terveydenhuollon työntekijät tarvitsevat täyden suojavarustuksen. Virusta vastaan ei ole hyväksyttyä rokotetta eikä tunnustettua lääkehoitoa. Nykyinen epidemia poikkeaa aiemmista Bundibugyo-epidemioista, joita havaittiin Ugandassa vuonna 2007 ja Kongon demokraattisessa tasavallassa vuonna 2012.

Turvattomuus estää sairastuneiden tavoittamista

Itäisen Kongon turvattomuus on vaikeuttanut torjuntatoimia epidemian keskuksessa. Janabin mukaan terveydenhuollon työntekijät tavoittavat vain noin 30 prosenttia tapauksista, kun muut sairastuneet kuolevat kotona. Torjuntaa hankaloittavat lisäksi perinteiset hautauskäytännöt, joissa surevat koskettavat vainajan ruumista, sekä joissakin yhteisöissä esiintyvä epäluulo terveysviranomaisia kohtaan. Kongon itäosiin on perustettu useita ebolapotilaiden hoitoon keskittyviä keskuksia, ja sairastuneet saavat nyt diagnoosin aiempaa nopeammin. Korkeina pysyvät tartuntamäärät osoittavat kuitenkin, etteivät viranomaiset ole vielä saaneet epidemian leviämistä hallintaan.
summary_bullets: Virus alkoi WHO:n mukaan levitä jo helmikuussa, mutta epidemia julistettiin virallisesti vasta 15. toukokuuta.
Elokuun 7. päivään mennessä oli vahvistettu 4 209 tartuntaa ja 1 916 kuolemaa.
Turvattomuus, rokotteen ja tunnustetun lääkehoidon puuttuminen sekä yhteisöjen epäluulo vaikeuttavat torjuntaa.
payload.journalist_note: Tapaus- ja kuolinluvut kuvaavat 7. elokuuta vallinnutta tilannetta ja voivat muuttua epidemian edetessä.
